sections.title: Employment Contract
sections.text:
Jacinta, who strives to live a life vivid enough, will never stop running forward.

She wants to go faster, and faster still — ideally, fast enough to outrun time itself.

sections.title: Token
sections.text: A calendar. For every place she visits and every goal she achieves, she adds another page. Once thin, this calendar grows ever thicker — just as her life grows ever more brilliant.

After Jacinta used her little parasol as a weapon and posted respectable scores in testing, Engineering Department operators who caught wind of it came by to give the parasol a thorough study.
The parasol, custom-made for her by her parents, is far more practical than it looks: the components inside launch automatically to attack enemies when the button on the handle is pressed; the ribs and canopy were forged through a special process that makes them remarkably tough; there is even a communicator tucked away out of sight that connects directly to her bodyguard team, more than enough to keep Jacinta safe... On top of that, the materials were chosen with Jacinta's stamina in mind, making it extremely light.
While the operators were still marveling at the parasol, Jacinta pulled a small folding fan out of somewhere inside it and fanned herself—so it accounts for that need too?

sections.title: Profile
sections.text: The daughter of the Campbells, renowned mining magnates of Rim Billiton, who came to Rhodes Island for Oripathy treatment. At her own request, she now assists Rhodes Island as a Vanguard Operator.

sections.title: Clinical Analysis
sections.text:
Imaging tests show the indistinct outlines of internal organs, obscured by abnormal shadows. Originium granules detected in the circulatory system. The subject is confirmed to be infected with Oripathy.

[Cell-Originium Assimilation] 13%
Small amounts of Originium crystals can be observed on the surface of Operator Jacinta's body.

[Blood Originium-Crystal Density] 0.41u/L
Operator Jacinta's condition has been kept well under control these past few years, but her prognosis remains far from optimistic.

After a series of physicals and tests, Medical Department operators found that Operator Jacinta's condition and overall physical state differed little from the thick stack of medical reports she had brought with her—though a few indicators, such as muscle mass and cardiopulmonary function, had improved markedly for reasons unknown.
The Medical Department operators had meant to ask what training could produce such results in just a few months, hoping to recommend it to every patient—but the answer they received was, “I crossed Rim Billiton. Twice.”

sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
Tall, quiet, gentle, her hem and collar spotlessly white and never out of place no matter the hour... Such is usually the first impression Operator Jacinta leaves on everyone, and everyone has kept things polite and friendly with her, worried that too much enthusiasm might offend or startle her. Until that day:
To brighten up the patients' lives, the Medical Department decided to hold a singing event in the garden, where anyone—patient or not—could sign up to take the stage and sing a favorite song. Sign-ups poured in, and Jacinta invited Thumpy to join her for the Rim Billiton folk song “Oh Woo Oh!” By the time their turn came it was nearly evening and the crowd's spirits had flagged a little, but the two of them still introduced themselves in high spirits and immediately let their voices loose—
According to an Engineering Department operator who was in another block entirely that day, she had been hurrying to finish a stability test on some equipment so she could go eat dinner, when for some reason her spirit level would not stop trembling. Utterly baffled, she finally decided to open a window for some air—and a piercing burst of song came barging into her ears: “A Cautus's ears~ Never fear the bending breeze~ Oh woo oh——! ♪”—at which point she understood exactly why her spirit level had been shaking, and, oddly taken with the singing, decided to go see for herself.
And so she found everyone in the garden holding hands, stomping through a ridiculous dance in complete disarray, howling with laughter. Up on stage Jacinta was in high spirits—though her volume was clearly no match for Thumpy's—belting out a song that kept teetering off-key, with not a trace of her usual composure.
The event ended with several encores of “Oh Woo Oh!” Everyone had a wonderful time—and once they knew Jacinta's “true face,” the number of operators dropping by to spend time with her multiplied several times over.

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
Rhodes Island's Medical Department recently received a sizable investment. With it, the department can more comfortably continue developing new drugs, expanding its production lines, and designing and upgrading medical equipment. That said, no sum of money ever appears out of nowhere:
Not long after Operator Jacinta joined Rhodes Island, a middle-aged couple arrived with a group of distinctly formidable-looking people in black and a group of doctors carrying every kind of medical instrument. They introduced themselves as the Campbells, Operator Jacinta's parents, along with her bodyguard and medical teams, come to visit Jacinta and to take charge of her safety and treatment aboard Rhodes Island.
And so, that day, Operator Jacinta showed her parents around her living areas—the dorms, the sickrooms, the cafeteria, and so on. The Campbells not only kept up a steady stream of reminders about what to watch out for, they also tried to negotiate with Human Resources: a bespoke plan for her food, clothing, lodging and travel as well as her treatment; a renovation of her dorm room; confirmation of the missions she would take on and the intensity of her training; and on, and on, and on... Just as the HR operator accompanying them was wondering whether to step in, Operator Jacinta beat her to it with a “mighty roar” that put a stop to the Campbells' endless fussing.
Contrary to the HR operator's fears, once Operator Jacinta showed the Campbells her certificates for every training program she had passed and her mission clearances, they did as she asked and withdrew the bodyguard and medical teams, choosing to trust and support the choice their daughter had made. Before leaving, though, they still wanted to look after her in their own way—and so, after a brief discussion, Rhodes Island's Medical Department suddenly received a sizable investment, to be used for medical research of every kind, all so that Operator Jacinta might be cared for that much better. On learning that running Rhodes Island requires an enormous amount of energy, the Campbells even sat down with Procurement to discuss future cooperation on ore purchases. Only after making certain that Rhodes Island had ample resources to take care of their daughter—and that Jacinta could take care of herself—did the Campbells finally set off back to Rim Billiton, satisfied at last.
Jacinta was overjoyed. After all these years of nothing but the sanatorium and the room at home that had been converted into a sickroom, she finally had a dorm of her own: not large, hardly well equipped, but the first room that belonged to her, the first she could decorate as she pleased—which also meant that she and her parents had found a new way of being with one another.
And of course, Warfarin and Closure—who had finally landed another deal—were delighted too!

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
Jacinta has a calendar.
At five, Jacinta got her first calendar. She did not buy it herself; her parents did, back when the doctors said she would not live another month. The Campbells filled it edge to edge with the times of Jacinta's treatments, her medications, their commemorative trips... In the end, though, the Campbells threw that calendar away. Those grueling years had left them exhausted; all they needed was to see that Jacinta was still alive, still under their protection.
At ten, Jacinta bought a calendar for herself. To safeguard her health, the Campbells had placed her in a sanatorium and hired all sorts of staff to handle her schooling, her daily life, her hobbies. In exchange, the ever-busy Campbells could not visit often, and Jacinta, whose health was poor, could not leave the center to go home for long. So she bought a calendar and marked down the days her parents came to see her. That calendar, too, she eventually threw away: their visits grew fewer and fewer, and Jacinta decided there was no need to keep such a record at all.
At nineteen, Jacinta found a calendar in her attending physician's office. It was unlike any other: the calendars for the next several years bound together into one, every page crammed with precautions, the last few pages shaded grey. Jacinta understood. That grey was the doctor's estimate of roughly how much time she had left. She went back to her room that day and wept until she had no tears left, then made an identical one for herself, tearing off a page each time a day passed—watching it grow thinner, and thinner, waiting for the day she would tear off the last page.
It was not as though she had never tried to run from the sanatorium before, but no one was willing to take a critically ill patient like her on the road, and her attempts and failures amounted to nothing more than small, unremarkable marks on the calendar. Then one day, Jacinta tore off a page as usual and realized that at some point the calendar had dwindled to a paper-thin remnant.
She had failed before, so trying once more was hardly a big deal. And if that was so—why not today? Jacinta pushed the door open and ran.
From the day she ran, Jacinta's calendar only grew thicker. Every commemorative photo, every map of a place she had been, even the receipt from a roadside meal or a pinch of shed fluff—she added them all in. When a day had passed and she went to tear off a page, countless little pieces of her life were already tucked in behind it.
Jacinta has a calendar, and that calendar is only getting thicker.

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
Once her treatment at Rhodes Island reached a stopping point, Jacinta set out on her travels.
Perhaps it was good luck, or perhaps it was because Jacinta never stopped thinking about the business she and Timeslot were starting, but she always seemed to find a way to pitch their product at the most unexpected moments.
Sightseeing in Sami, she lent a mobile signal base station—brought along purely for testing—to a rescue team, and the trapped were pulled out safely. Filming videos with Click sent her likes and follower count through the roof and drew inquiries from more than a few media companies. She even set out with Aurora to climb a snowy mountain—wisely giving up the ascent in the end, given her physical condition—and still ran into Rhine Lab staff, placing Amelia's business card into the hands of the great Columbian company Amelia so admired. When the news reached her, Amelia was in happy tears every single day.
That said, not everything Jacinta ran into on her travels had to do with the business she and Timeslot were starting.
As an Oripathy patient herself, Jacinta knew that some things are genuinely hard to handle, hard to resolve. That day, at the foot of the snowy mountain, Jacinta came across someone dressed far too thinly for the cold. Originium crystals had spread across her skin, and every step tore at flesh until blood seeped through; anyone could see she was critically ill. The mountain was only an ordinary peak among the snowfields, but the people nearby lived off it and had gradually come to revere it, and perhaps the woman was there to pray for blessings. Jacinta knew, however, that this would do her no good whatsoever beyond irreversible damage to her health. The villagers around her told Jacinta that the woman had gone mad and that she had best keep her distance—they had never once spoken to her.
She stayed with that person at the foot of the mountain for three days. At first Jacinta kept trying to talk her round, offering to share her own medicine and food, pitching a tent for her, contacting operators at the Rhodes Island office for aid—but the woman never said a word. Once Jacinta saw that her spirit was flagging further still, she stopped trying to persuade her. She simply sat a little way off, keeping her company in silence, now and then feeding the fire in front of them so that they would both be a little more comfortable.
When the sun rose on the fourth day, the woman's tent was empty. All Jacinta found inside was a strip of bark, a single small line written on it in ash: “Thank you for staying with me.” Far off, in a cave, she found the traces left behind when the woman disintegrated.
“At least she wasn't all alone at the end...” To the medic operator's surprise, Jacinta was perfectly calm as she spoke of it.

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
......
We were the narrow-minded ones. It never once occurred to us that you could be this brave. We believed that keeping you alive was the best thing for you, and in doing so we ignored your pain—and... ignored our own pain as well.
I don't want to say too much in a letter, in case you take it the wrong way. I only want to tell you that heaven knows how thrilled we were to receive the photograph of you down in the South—you really did it!
Back in Big Iron, it was your mother who told me she had never seen you as happy as you were behind the wheel that night. I half believed her at the time—I thought your mother was simply taking your side... But in the South you truly did look happy. Since you fell ill, it had been such a long, long time since I last saw you smile like that. Far too long. And that is my fault.
Our brave little one, our daughter—thank you for giving yourself a whole new life, and thank you for giving me the chance to take a good, hard look at myself again.
I'm sorry.
Thank you.
You will always be our pride.
—Your father
